1:
The title sets off the quarrel that runs through the whole commentary. Charles Ellicott begins with the grammar: the phrase might mean one song out of a collection of a thousand and five, but since Hebrew marks a definite compound idea by the article on the second word, it means the surpassing song. John Gill reaches the same sense by the parallel of the Holy of holies and the King of kings, and Adam Clarke by the God of gods and heaven of heavens; John Wesley takes the superlative three ways, of the author, the subject and the matter, which he says breathes the hottest flames of love. Matthew Henry divides the title into nature, dignity and penman: a song, because the design is to stir and heat the affections, which poetry does; the most excellent of songs, as having more of Christ in it than any other; and not the song of fools, as many songs of love are, but the song of the wisest of men.

On what kind of book it is, the answers separate. Keil and Delitzsch open by calling it the most obscure book of the Old Testament, since on any principle of interpretation inexplicable passages remain, and just those that would solve the mystery if understood; interpreting it is an ungrateful task, they add, since the interpreter is thanked for the parts only if his conception of the whole is approved. It is a love-poem, they say, and ask why such a poem stands in the canon: the question raised doubts in the Jewish schools of the first century, answered by presupposing that the love was spiritual and reading it allegorically, as the Targum did in making it the history of a nation from the Exodus to the coming of Messiah. Clarke asks the question of genre precisely, defining ode, idyl, pastoral and marriage-song and finding the book falls under none; it is of its own kind, he decides, most like a mask, an entertainment for wedding guests with a dramatic cast, and he wonders whether the English poet who wrote one took the idea from this.

Clarke then dissents from nearly everyone, at length and by name. He lists six opinions held about the book, from a plain marriage-song for a foreign princess to an allegory of the incarnation, and observes that antiquity is no evidence of truth, since many ungodly opinions are more than a thousand years old, and that great names are enrolled on every side. His own argument is from silence: the name of God is not in the book, and it is not quoted in the New Testament, whereas if it set out the love of Christ for the church the apostles would not have passed it over. He names the interpreters he refuses, Gill among those he lists as having laboured to prove that it concerns Christ and the elect. After nearly fifty years of reading it at intervals, he says, he sees in this Hebrew ode nothing of Christ and his church, and holds that the spiritualising of it has propagated a mean and carnal language among well-meaning religious people.

The others write as though the question were settled. Gill takes Solomon for the writer against the tradition that gives the book to a later king and his men, and reports a saying that wherever the name of Solomon occurs here the Holy One is meant. Wesley states flatly that the subject is not Solomon but a greater than Solomon, and Henry calls the book evangelical, since gospel times should be times of joy. Clarke alone dates it: not a work of old age, since the writer then had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines while the Song names sixty and eighty; and he reports that some rabbins gave the book to Isaiah. Ellicott settles nothing here, referring authorship and date to an excursus elsewhere.
2:
The poem begins without an antecedent, and all of them notice it. Matthew Henry compares the woman at the sepulchre who said, if thou have borne him hence, meaning Christ without naming him, and observes that those full of Christ are ready to think others must be so too. John Wesley defends the abruptness as proper to writing of this kind, where things are not told in order, citing Homer and Virgil. John Gill calls it a relative whose antecedent was only in her own mind; Adam Clarke makes it modesty, that she speaks of the bridegroom in the third person out of respect. When the person changes in the next clause, Wesley calls the shift frequent in pathetic discourse, Charles Ellicott a figure common in sacred poetry.

The second clause divides on a vowel. Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek read thy breasts for thy love, having the defectively written word before them, and Clarke that the versions generally do so, the two being said to stand for the Old and New Testaments. Ellicott calls it the origin of many fanciful interpretations, one making the breasts the two Testaments which breathe love, the first promising and the second revealing Christ, and condemns it because the words are spoken not to a woman but by one. A second variant follows: many prefer let him give me to drink for let him kiss me, which Ellicott grants preserves the metaphor of the wine, quoting an English lyric about leaving a kiss in the cup and asking for no wine; Keil and Delitzsch refuse it, since to give to drink with kisses is an expression without support. They also read the opening word as partitive, so that the speaker is one among many to whom the kisses are distributed.

The ointment and the name are the hardest grammar here. Keil and Delitzsch dispute with three interpreters over whether the word means the smell given off or the sense of smell, and add that the song was sung where wine was presented and perfumes sprinkled, the love of the host set above both. Ellicott finds the difficulties enough to make a literal rendering doubtful, divides the verse into three clauses rather than two, prefers to make the name the thing poured out like oil, and points out the play between the Hebrew words for oil and name. Gill keeps to custom, that lovers anointed themselves and commended each other’s perfumes. Clarke reads the last clause as modesty again, since by the virgins she means herself. Ellicott reports the other possibility without softening it, that those who take the king for the object of these verses understand the word of the ladies of the harem.

At the drawing the accents decide. Keil and Delitzsch note that all recent interpreters render draw me after thee, so we run, but that the accentuation requires the older division, draw me, so will we run after thee, the verb needing no complement, its root meaning to lay hold and hold fast. Henry reads it as doctrine: the petition implies distance felt and union desired, and since we are not only weak but naturally backward we must pray for the grace by which the unwilling are made willing, yet are not driven to Christ but drawn in a way agreeable to rational creatures. Wesley draws from the change of number that the spouse is one great body of many members. Gill reports an interpreter who gives the words to the virgins. Ellicott sets the verse in the argument about the shape of the book, since the dramatic theory has been largely built on it, and reads the clause about the king as a supposition: even should the king have brought me into his chambers, our joys are for thee alone. Clarke takes it plainly, that her spouse is a potentate and no ordinary person.
5:
Black but comely is explained by climate, lineage and grace. Adam Clarke takes it as plain description, true of many Asiatic women, who though brown are exquisitely beautiful; the tents are tawny and the pavilions probably covered with a tanned cloth. Charles Ellicott reads the comparisons as a parallelism, dark as tents of black goats’ hair and beautiful as the royal hangings, and calls it playful raillery immediately redeemed by a compliment. Keil and Delitzsch infer from her calling the women daughters of the city that she came from elsewhere, and name the district, adding, in the interest of the mystical interpretation, that the first congregations of the church were from the same one. John Gill divides the words between two views of her, black in herself and to the world, comely in the eyes of Christ. John Wesley notices that the last two clauses answer the first two in the same order, and refers the blackness to the foreign princess.

Clarke then says out loud what the chapter has been circling: the women of the city are said to represent the synagogue and the bride the church, he reports, adding that it is easy to find spiritual meanings, since every creed will furnish them. On the sunburn he keeps to history: a foreigner brought to the throne would excite jealousy among the women of that country, who might think their king should not have gone abroad for a wife. Ellicott turns the verse against that theory: her darkness is accidental, got by working out of doors, and cannot prove her a foreign princess at all. He glosses her mother’s children as brothers and not step-brothers, notes that naming the mother is natural where polygamy is practised, and on the vineyard she did not keep lists the guesses, her beloved, her reputation, her own vine, before taking the obvious sense, that her appearance was sacrificed to her brothers’ severity. Keil and Delitzsch make the word a diminutive, blackish, dark here and there rather than altogether black. Wesley alone allegorises the brothers into false brethren.

At the noon question the pastoral setting is pressed. Clarke suggests that the marriage festival included something like our masks, in which persons of quality took rural characters, and refers again to an English poem of that kind; he explains that shepherds in hot countries must shelter at midday, and quotes a Latin eclogue on herdsmen driving their flocks together to sing. Matthew Henry takes the title she gives, the one whom my soul loveth, for the undoubted character of every believer, and finds both repast and repose provided for the sheep. Wesley reads noon as the time of persecution, when the true church is hard to discover, and the companions’ flocks as the assemblies of corrupt teachers.

The last clause of the seventh verse is the crux, and the eighth divides them. Ellicott reports that the margin follows the Greek in rendering it veiled, rejects the senses proposed for it, unknown, veiled as a harlot and fainting, and prefers a wandering got by transposing two letters, the idea being to go about blindfold. He also quotes a rabbinic exposition of the verse as an instance of the fanciful treatment this book has received. At the reply Clarke says the virgins answer, not knowing exactly and directing her to the shepherds. Ellicott marks the verse as the end of a subsection, notes that supporters of the dramatic theory begin a new scene after it, and that many read the answer as the court ladies mocking her low birth, though he takes it as playful. Keil and Delitzsch settle the vocative as a superlative and add that a face judged not beautiful is judged otherwise as soon as its owner speaks. Gill cites a father for the claim that the maxim about knowing oneself was not the oracle’s first, Solomon having it before and from Moses.
9:
The comparison to a horse embarrasses the commentary. Adam Clarke renders it more literally, to my mare in the chariots of Pharaoh, and explains that mares were preferred in the East as swifter and hardier; then he answers the objection with a Greek idyl in which the most beautiful woman of antiquity is likened to a horse in a chariot, quoting the lines and translating them. Charles Ellicott makes the same defence with three poets instead of one, and adds that an Arab chief would not hesitate to prefer the points of his horse to the charms of his mistress; he notes that some, offended by the comparison, suppose the trappings of the royal equipage suggested it, and rules out the suppositions that the plural points to one particular team and that the animals were a present between monarchs. John Wesley avoids the difficulty by making the likeness one of strength and courage, the church being fair but also terrible to her enemies. John Gill spends his note on the address, that my love and my friend are names used between lovers, and that the Greek has my neighbour.

Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to stage the scene. Solomon, absent through the first part, is now present and speaking; the woman has been alone with the ladies of the palace, who are still there but out of hearing; and the word he uses of her is one of friendship, since she is not yet his bride. The first words she speaks to him, they note, come only at the following verse.

On the jewels they turn to travel writing. Clarke quotes a traveller on the Arabian women, who wear pearls about the neck and cap and gold chains on the bosom, with coins fastened along the forehead and both cheeks, the poorer sort covering the forehead-piece with silver pieces like fish scales; and he adds that he has seen their scent bottles ornamented with festoons of small coins and beads, and that one lies before him as he writes. Ellicott quotes two travellers to the same effect, one on the coins strung round the forehead and over a network falling to the waist, another on the Persian ladies whose rows of pearls hang down the cheeks so that their faces seem set in pearls; and he adds an English lady’s description of a sultana wearing four strings of great pearls. He also settles the words: the first comes from a root meaning to go round, so that it means circlets or the beads themselves, the second means perforated, that is, beads or coins strung together.

Gill takes the ornaments as turtledoves, following the Greek, and reconstructs them: an earring fastened to a plate of gold or a ribbon across the forehead, hanging down by the ears on both cheeks, with a further jewel from the same plate falling to the nose; and he identifies it with what was put on the face of the patriarch’s bride at the well. Wesley remarks only that the cheeks are named as the chief seat of beauty. On the golden borders the readings divide. Gill hears Christ speaking in his own name and in the name of the other two divine Persons, and takes the gold and silver for the ordinances and doctrines of the Gospel, the studs for its precious promises. Wesley makes the plural the Son and the Father. Ellicott reports what the dramatic theory does with the verse, turning it into a seductive offer of richer ornaments to dazzle a rustic girl, and answers that no theory is needed to explain a lover wishing to adorn his beloved. Matthew Henry keeps the ornaments as figures of grace, the gifts of Christ being many and dependent on each other, and adds that it is Christ himself and not his gifts who is precious to believers.
12:
The king at his table is placed by some and dismissed by one. Adam Clarke renders the phrase in his circle, meaning the circle of friends at the festival or a round table, and John Gill takes it the same way, alluding to the round tables the ancients used. Charles Ellicott uses the verse to refuse a whole scene: there is no need, he says, to imagine the monarch, having failed to allure the shepherdess with fine offers, retiring to his banquet while she consoles herself with thoughts of an absent shepherd. Matthew Henry spreads the table in the gospel, where the king sits to see his guests, to welcome them and to carve for them. On the perfume Ellicott turns botanist: the spikenard is exclusively an Indian product, got from a plant of the valerian order and imported very early, the scent prepared by drying the shaggy stem. John Wesley keeps to the custom of the feast, where such ointments were poured on the guests’ heads, spikenard being a chief ingredient.

At the bundle of myrrh Keil and Delitzsch take issue with almost everyone. Most interpreters, they say, ignore the lessons of botany and explain the words of a little bunch of myrrh; but where would she have got one? The plant is an exotic there, its aromatic part is resin, and resin cannot be tied in a bunch. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from custom, citing a scholar who quotes an early rabbinic code for the practice of wearing sachets or bottles of myrrh hung from the neck; and he sets beside the verse an English song about wishing to be the necklace that rises and falls on the beloved and is scarcely unclasped at night. Gill describes the same bottle, liquid myrrh carried in the bosom as people carry smelling bottles, and reports that some take the plant for sweet marjoram. Clarke passes on another writer’s point, that it is the bundle of myrrh and not the beloved that lies all night between the breasts, the comparison being to its continual fragrance.

The cluster of the next verse is the hardest identification here, and four attempt it. Ellicott has no doubt: the word is the henna of the Arabs, and he names the botanists’ term for it; a traveller found it growing in abundance at that one place and proposed the identification, another describes it as a shrub eight or ten feet high with clusters of white and yellow blossoms of powerful fragrance, from whose dried and pounded leaves a paste is made with which women of all ranks dye the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. He notes that a third writer prefers a favourite kind of grape, and gives no sufficient reason for it. Gill argues the other way: the place was famous for palm trees, a Roman naturalist calling it second only to the capital for fertility, a historian saying the best palms and balsam grew there, so that Jewish writers took the clusters for dates; what we call camphire cannot be meant, since it does not grow in clusters and was unknown to the ancients. Clarke reports a proposal that it is a bunch of the grape of a certain island, then offers his own guess, that the poet means the dark colour of the hair, which the Greeks compared to bunches of grapes and which he calls no unfit similitude for thick black clustering curls, quoting a couplet on locks hanging like the branchy palm. Wesley declines the question, saying we are not concerned to know exactly what the plant was, since it is confessed to have been some grateful thing that sets forth the delight of the church in Christ. Keil and Delitzsch mark the effect of all this on the hearer, that in such ardour of devotion she must appear to the king the more beautiful.
15:
At the praise of the eyes the chapter changes speaker, and one voice says how little that settles. Charles Ellicott observes that the song is now transferred to a male speaker, and that the advocates of the dramatic theory cannot agree whether it is the king or the shepherd, which is no wonder, since the poem gives no indication; the terms of endearment, he adds, cannot safely be pressed for any theory. He counts the doves instead: of about fifty mentions of the bird in Scripture, seven fall within this short book, so that it is especially dear to this poet; and he sets two English poets beside the phrase, one on the doves’ eyes that can make gods forsworn. Adam Clarke identifies the bird as the large and beautiful dove of the country, whose eyes are remarkably fine. John Wesley makes the comparison moral, since doves are mild and harmless, chaste and faithful, and takes the eyes for both the outward behaviour and the inward disposition. John Gill works on the opening word, taking it as a note of attention, calling her to consider her comeliness in Christ rather than pore on her own blackness; of admiration, that one so uncomely in herself should be beautiful in his eyes; and of asseveration, assuring her of what she would be apt to call in question.

The answering verse is where Keil and Delitzsch make their stand. If this were not her echo to the king, they say, but addressed to another man, the poet must have used a different demonstrative; and they answer the scholar who reads the first words as mere politeness and the added word charming as distinguishing her true beloved from a king she cannot bear. If a man and a woman are together, they reply, and he says the one thing and she says the other, that is as certainly an interchange of address as that one and one are two and not three. They add what follows about her, that her happiness is at home among her own rural scenes and the city with its noisy display does not please her. Ellicott says the same in a clause, that she recalls the happy woodland places where they used to meet. Gill takes the whole verse as her giving his commendation back to him, and marks the difference, that his fairness is essential and underived while hers is all from him. Wesley makes the retort sharper still: thou, and thou only, art fair indeed.

The green bed and the cedar beams are read as furniture or as landscape. Clarke says the word generally means a mattress, but here is probably a green bank on which they sat, being out on a walk, or else a bower or the nuptial bed; and at the beams he supposes a cedar whose limbs were interwoven with a tree of the cypress kind, a natural bower recommending itself by its strength and by the shade it gave. He closes the chapter with a stage note, that with it the first day of the marriage ceremonies is supposed to end. Ellicott reaches the same picture by the word for rafters, from a root meaning to run or flow, which yields a gutter, a curl and here the beams that spread overhead; others read a transposed form explained as turned work, but the thought is plainly connected with the woods and not with a gorgeous house, the couch being green grass, the arches of the bower cedar branches and its rafters firs. Gill turns the house into the congregation and its beams into the ministers and members who support it, cedar being fragrant and durable as their grace is lasting. Wesley notes only that cedar and cypress are alike strong and fragrant and so suit each other.
